passage:
Monday. Keya had spent the weekend on her first market report. Asif glanced through it at his desk, phone pressed to his ear, and slid it back. "Redo this. Tighter." Then he turned away to his call.
Tuesday. She rewrote the summary four times, not sure what 'tighter' meant. Was it the numbers? The length? Every time Asif walked past, she opened her mouth to ask and closed it again. At lunch Karthik, the other intern, said, "He's like that with everyone." She wasn't sure she believed him.
Thursday. She submitted the new version at 11 p.m., stomach tight, and lay awake wondering whether she'd already failed the internship, or whether Asif had simply had no time to explain.

qa.q: What one word did Asif use to say how Keya should redo the report?
qa.a: Tighter.

qa.q: Why did Keya keep opening her mouth to ask and then closing it?
qa.a: She was afraid asking would show she wasn't good enough 😰, and she couldn't tell if Asif was displeased or just busy.

qa.q: What small step could change things for Keya at this early stage?
qa.a: She could ask one specific question, like 'Is it the length or the numbers?', which is normal for an intern and would replace guessing with facts.

qa.q: What might Asif have been dealing with when he slid the report back?
qa.a: He was on a phone call and seemed rushed, so he may not have realised how little his one word explained or how it would land.

grounding: Over a week a woman intern told to redo a report with one word feels criticised, unsure if she failed or the senior is busy, and is afraid to ask.

passage: Aditi, you look exactly like I did at your age, staring at that email. Let your Zainab Aunty tell you something. I was twenty, an intern at a newspaper in Hyderabad. The chief sub-editor, Mr Reddy, pushed my first story back across the desk. 'Do it again.' Nothing else. I went to the washroom and cried, then rewrote it three times, guessing. Was my English bad? Did he think I was stupid? I was too scared to go and ask. Only months later did I learn he'd had four pages to close that night and barely read past my first line. So don't do what I did, beta. Go and ask your senior what was meant.

qa.q: What did Mr Reddy say when he pushed Zainab's first story back?
qa.a: He said, 'Do it again.' Nothing else.

qa.q: What was young Zainab afraid of as she rewrote the story three times?
qa.a: She feared her English was bad or that he thought she was stupid, and that fear kept her from simply asking.

qa.q: What advice does Zainab give Aditi, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To go and ask what the senior meant, because a busy senior's short words may have little to do with Aditi, and asking ends the guessing.

qa.q: What was that night like for Mr Reddy, as Zainab later learned?
qa.a: He had four pages to close and barely read past her first line, so his curt words came from pressure rather than judgement of her.

grounding: An aunt recalls being a young intern told to redo work without explanation, feeling criticised, unsure why, and too scared to ask.

passage:
Naveen, I swear, Farhan sir hates me. Every time I send him something he replies in one line: 'Fine.' 'Fix slide 4.' 'Noted.' No hello, no thanks. With the other interns he jokes, but with me it's all business. So I just keep my head down in meetings and don't say anything. Why give him more to dislike?
Then yesterday Rimjhim told me he'd asked her, 'Is Sanjana even interested in this role? She never asks a single question.' Interested? I'm staying back till eight!
I thought quiet meant respectful. He thinks it means I don't care. And I thought short meant he hates me. Maybe it just means he's drowning in emails, like everyone. I don't know.

qa.a: She is staying back till eight.

qa.a: He seems to read it as lack of interest, not realising she is quiet out of respect and fear, and he may not notice how brisk his replies sound.

passage: I'm Lakshmi, and I sit between Bidisha's desk and Mr Rao's cabin at the accounts firm, so I see both sides. Mr Rao talks to everyone in bullet points: 'Ledger. Today. Thanks.' He doesn't mean anything by it; he's been like that for fifteen years. But Bidisha, who joined in June, flinches every time. She's stopped asking him anything and just quietly guesses. Last week in the tea room Mr Rao said to me, 'That new girl doesn't seem very interested. Never asks a thing.' The same afternoon Bidisha whispered, 'He can't stand me, can he?' I didn't know what to tell either of them. I think they're both wrong. Nobody explains, and nobody asks.

qa.a: Bidisha joined in June.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's whisper 'He can't stand me, can he?' reveal about how she reads Mr Rao?
qa.a: She takes his brisk bullet-point style as personal dislike, and she seems anxious and hurt by it.

qa.q: How could someone like Lakshmi gently help at this stage?

qa.a: He reads her silence as lack of interest, not realising his short style has made her afraid to ask.

passage: Monday's team meeting in the Osaka office had nine people around the table. Yuki-san was going through the client figures when the slide stopped on Aiko's chart. "This total is wrong. Aiko, you've counted March twice." A few heads turned. Aiko felt heat climb from her neck to her ears. She'd checked it. Hadn't she? She opened her mouth, then pressed her lips together and bowed slightly. "I'm sorry. I'll fix it." The meeting moved on. That evening on the crowded train home, and later in the shower, she kept replaying it. I could have said, 'Thank you, I'll send a corrected version by noon.' Or, 'Could we go over it after the meeting?' Anything but that small bow.

qa.q: What error did Yuki-san point out in Aiko's chart?
qa.a: Aiko had counted March twice.

qa.q: What was Aiko feeling as heat climbed from her neck to her ears?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and exposed in front of nine people, with a flash of doubt about whether she really had checked it.

qa.q: What could Aiko do next to move on from this moment?
qa.a: Rather than only replaying it, she could fix the figure and ask Yuki-san for a short private word about checking totals, turning the sting into learning.

qa.q: What might the correction have been like from Yuki-san's side?
qa.a: Yuki-san may simply have wanted the figures right for the client and not noticed how a public correction felt to a new intern.

grounding: A young woman is corrected in front of her team, feels her face burn, swallows her reply and spends the evening rehearsing better ones.

passage: The Friday staff meeting at the Indore school was running late. Vaibhav sir, the senior maths teacher, held up the Class 7 test paper Yamini had set. "Question five has two correct answers. The trainee should have had it checked." Twelve teachers looked at her. Yamini's face burned. She'd given it to him on Tuesday to check, and he hadn't said anything. The words were right there, but she swallowed them and nodded. That night, grading copies at her kitchen table, she said the sentence out loud to the empty room: "I did give it to you on Tuesday, sir." Then a calmer version. Then a sharper one. By midnight she'd rehearsed six replies and used none of them.

qa.a: Question five had two correct answers.

qa.q: Why did Yamini say the sentence out loud to the empty room that night?

qa.q: What might be a wise next step for Yamini after this public correction?
qa.a: She could ask Vaibhav sir for a short private talk, calmly mention she shared it on Tuesday, and ask how checking should work in future.

qa.q: What might the other teachers have thought when they saw Yamini nod silently?
qa.a: Some may have assumed she made a careless mistake, while others might have noticed her burning face and felt uneasy about the public correction.

grounding: A trainee teacher is corrected in front of the staff, swallows her reply and spends the night rehearsing what she could have said.

passage: At lunch in the Dublin office, Emeka slid his tray next to Ngozi's. "Liam tore into you in stand-up. You should hear what the rest of us say about him." Ngozi shook her head. She'd spent the night angry, but by morning she'd written three sentences on a sticky note. At three o'clock she knocked on Liam's glass door. "Have you got five minutes?" He looked surprised. She kept her voice steady. "I want to get this right. Could you tell me what I should improve in the forecast? And when possible, could feedback come privately?" Liam leaned back, quiet for a second. "That's fair. Sit down. Let's go through it now." When she came out twenty minutes later, her notebook was full.

qa.q: Where had Ngozi written her three sentences?
qa.a: She had written them on a sticky note.

qa.q: Why did Ngozi shake her head at Emeka's offer?
qa.a: She was still hurt but wanted to fix the problem rather than feed gossip, choosing calm action over venting with peers.

qa.q: Which parts of Ngozi's request made it likely to be welcomed?
qa.a: She asked for a short private talk, led with wanting to improve, asked for specifics, and made one clear, polite request about private feedback.

qa.q: How might Liam see Ngozi after this conversation?
qa.a: He probably sees her as professional and serious about the work 🙂, and may think twice before correcting her publicly again.

grounding: Instead of venting with peers, a young woman asks her senior for a private talk about what to improve and for private feedback, and he welcomes it.

passage: The state library's digitisation room hummed with scanners. After Wednesday's review, where Darshan sir had called her file names 'a mess' in front of the whole team, Urmila's fellow interns were ready to rant in the group chat. She typed, deleted, and closed the app. On Thursday morning she waited until he was alone at the catalogue desk. "Sir, could I have ten minutes today?" At four they sat by the window. "I want to do this well," she said, hands folded to keep them still. "Could you show me exactly what's wrong with the file names? And if possible, could corrections like that come privately?" Darshan sir blinked, then nodded slowly. "Fair. I should have shown you the format first." He pulled out a printed sheet.

qa.q: Where did Urmila wait to find Darshan sir alone?
qa.a: She waited until he was alone at the catalogue desk.

qa.q: What does Urmila folding her hands to keep them still suggest?
qa.a: She was nervous about raising it, yet determined to stay calm and speak clearly.

qa.q: Why was Urmila's choice better than ranting in the group chat?
qa.a: Talking privately and calmly gave Darshan sir a chance to explain and change, while venting would only have spread resentment without fixing anything.

qa.q: What might Darshan sir realise when he says he should have shown her the format first?
qa.a: He seems to see that his public criticism skipped a step, and that the intern needed guidance before correction.

grounding: A young woman intern skips the group-chat rant and calmly asks her senior privately for specifics and for private feedback.

passage: Mateo was locking up the Madrid co-working office when he saw Fatima's corrected brief still on the printer. He'd marked it up in the Thursday meeting, loudly, in front of everyone: 'This isn't how we format client briefs.' Now, reading her neat new version, he remembered something uncomfortable. Nobody had ever given her the template. He'd assumed she knew it because he'd known it for three years. He thought of her face in that meeting, very still, eyes on the table. On Monday he stopped by her desk. "About Thursday. The format still needs to be like this; that's not changing. But I pointed it out badly, in front of everyone, and without ever showing you the template. That was on me. Sorry." Fatima looked up, surprised.

qa.q: What had nobody ever given Fatima?
qa.a: Nobody had ever given her the template.

qa.q: What did Mateo feel when he remembered Fatima's still face in the meeting?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising he had been careless with her dignity by assuming she knew the standard.

qa.q: What makes Mateo's apology on Monday a good one?
qa.a: He keeps the correction, since the format still matters, while owning how he said it and the missing template, so the standard stays and her dignity is repaired.

qa.q: What might Fatima be feeling as she looks up, surprised?
qa.a: She may feel relief and fresh respect for Mateo now that he has admitted his part without taking back the feedback.

grounding: A young senior realises he assumed a new colleague knew the standard and embarrassed her, and apologises for the manner while keeping the correction.

passage: After the late-night bulletin, the radio station studio was empty except for Hemant and Vasudha, the programme head. "Parul's script was weak. I'll stand by that," Hemant said, packing his headphones. Vasudha raised an eyebrow. "And how you said it? In the corridor, with guests walking past?" Hemant opened his mouth, then shut it. He remembered Parul's hands shaking as she took the pages back. He'd assumed she knew the station style; he'd never actually shown it to her. The next morning he found Parul at the coffee machine. "Your script still needs cutting to ninety seconds. That part stands. But I shouldn't have said it in the corridor, and I should've given you our style sheet first. I'm sorry." He handed her a printed page.

"Actually good," Meenal said. "Ritesh sir and I have a Monday check-in now. Fifteen minutes. And he wrote down what a finished report should look like. One page."

passage: Three months into my internship, I, Leela, finally understand what happened with Chetan. For weeks I'd been the quiet new girl, sitting on my resentment: the public corrections, the one-word emails. After we talked privately, we tried something simple. Every Friday at four, ten minutes at his desk. And a shared document titled 'What done looks like', where he wrote the standard for every task before I started it. The first Friday felt stiff. By the fourth, I was bringing my own list of questions, and he was asking what I thought. Last week he disagreed with my plan, and I said, 'I see it differently,' out loud, in a meeting. He said, 'Good point, let's try yours.' Swallowing it never got me that. Saying it respectfully did.

qa.q: What was the shared document titled?
qa.a: It was titled 'What done looks like'.

qa.q: How did Leela feel during the first Friday check-in compared with the fourth?
qa.a: The first felt stiff and awkward, but by the fourth she felt confident enough to bring her own questions, suggesting growing trust.

qa.q: Why did the weekly check-in and shared document help?
qa.a: They made expectations clear before work began and gave a regular, safe place to raise problems, so resentment didn't build up.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Leela now compared with before?
qa.a: He probably sees her as a contributor whose views are worth hearing, since he now asks her opinion and accepted her plan.

grounding: A young woman looks back on how a weekly check-in and written standards turned swallowed resentment into respectful disagreement and trust.

passage:
Team lead's note, Anjali, after Tuesday's client review.
Pritam presented the logistics dashboard today. It went well. But the credits slide listed only his name, and Joseph built the entire data pipeline behind it. The two had overlapped on this project because I never split the roles clearly; that part is on me.
I watched Joseph during the presentation. He stopped taking notes after the credits slide and looked at the window for the rest of the hour. Afterwards he said to me, 'It's fine,' in a voice that wasn't fine. When I asked Pritam, he looked genuinely startled: 'I just used last month's template. I didn't think.'
Next: talk to each of them separately this week, then write clear role notes on the project sheet.

passage:
Wednesday, 10:40 p.m.
Deepak presented the pricing model to the directors today. Our pricing model. I built half the formulas and every single test case. His slides had one name at the bottom: his. I sat in the back row, clapping with everyone else, feeling like a stranger at my own project.
Afterwards I said, as lightly as I could, 'Nice job. Missed my name, though.' He actually laughed. 'Oh no, sorry yaar, total oversight, I made the deck in a rush.' Maybe it was. Our roles on this were never really clear.
But can you really 'forget' months of someone's work?
Ma called and asked why her son sounded so flat. I said I was tired. Why does it sting so much?
- Vikas

passage: I'm Rukmini, and I share a pod with Kamal and Harish. After the quarterly review where Harish presented the vendor plan alone, Kamal said nothing in the meeting. Not a word. He's so cold with me.' I don't know what Kamal feels inside. I only know the room has gone quiet between them.

passage: Looking back, I, Wasim, can see how fast it spread. It started as a quarrel between Rehana and Tushar about who owned the vendor project. Within two weeks the lunch table had split: Rehana's side by the window, Tushar's by the fridge. Someone made a chat group without Tushar in it, then another without Rehana. I was in both, and said different things in each. Shameful, honestly. Devika, our manager, clearly felt something was off. She asked in a meeting, 'Is everything okay with the team?' Nobody said a word. So the guesses started: that Rehana wanted Devika's job, that Tushar was leaving, that Devika played favourites. None of it was true. The one true thing, the project quarrel, nobody ever told her.

passage:
Manager's note, Elizabeth, Friday.
Something is wrong on the design team and I can't see what. Three signs this week. The Thursday lunch table, which used to be one long noisy row, has split in two. When I walked into the kitchen, Anjali and two others stopped talking. And a junior told me, awkwardly, that there's 'a group chat drama', then refused to say more.
I've now heard three different theories: that Anjali is being pushed out, that I favour the senior designers, that someone complained to HR. None came from the people actually involved.
What I did: asked each team member for fifteen minutes one-to-one next week, with one open question, 'What's making work harder right now?' No names needed. I want the cause, not the rumours.

passage: Madhuri, you won't believe what I did today. The launch deadline slipped, and in the review meeting Tarun said, in front of the director, 'Some of us needed the copy on Monday and got it Thursday.' Some of us! My face went hot and I snapped back: 'Some of us sent three reminders for the brief and got nothing.' Then he raised his voice, and I raised mine, and the director had to say, 'Enough, both of you.' Twelve people staring. I can't even remember how it ended. And now? I'm furious that he humiliated me, and he's probably telling everyone I humiliated him. We both think the other crossed a line. Honestly, maybe we both did. But I'm not apologising first. I'm Vandana, not a doormat.

qa.a: Three reminders.

qa.q: Why won't Vandana apologise first?
qa.a: Vandana feels humiliated in front of twelve people and believes Tarun crossed a line, so apologising first feels like losing face.

qa.q: What turning point might still be possible after this open clash?
qa.a: Once both cool down, a private talk, perhaps with the director or a neutral person, could sort out the brief-and-copy timeline instead of trading public blame.

qa.q: How might Tarun be seeing the same meeting?
qa.a: He likely feels just as embarrassed and blamed, believing Vandana disrespected him in front of the director.
